counterfactuals.possibleOutcome: the documented six-minute detection might not have occurred at that time.

counterfactuals.condition: If the automated rule had not halted expansion,
counterfactuals.possibleOutcome: the model could have expanded beyond the initial exposure despite the 14-point segment decline.

counterfactuals.condition: If the affected segment could not have been disabled independently,
counterfactuals.possibleOutcome: the response described in the evidence—disabling only that segment while retaining service elsewhere—would not have been available.

counterfactuals.condition: If pre-release tests had included a case capable of exposing this defect,
counterfactuals.possibleOutcome: the segment-specific failure might have been detected before deployment.

counterfactuals.condition: If the team had not practiced rollback,
counterfactuals.possibleOutcome: the effect on response speed or correctness is unknown.

output.summary: Three refrigerated containers exceeded the product temperature limit during a six-hour transfer (E1). The evidence points to a conjunctive cause: sensor calibration drift that appeared only above 88% relative humidity (E2), a condition present for 73 minutes of the transfer (E5), combined with a firmware retry defect that made the compressor controller ignore every second restart command after a communications timeout (E3). Two comparison runs isolate the factors: the firmware defect alone with calibrated sensors stayed within limit (E6), and the sensor drift alone with corrected restart logic stayed within limit (E7). Neither factor is sufficient on its own within this evidence; together they coincide with the exceedance. A separate alerting rule suppressed repeat temperature alerts for 45 minutes after first acknowledgement (E4), which extended operator response after the limit had already been crossed (E8) — an exposure-duration factor, not a cause of the crossing. The package does not state the direction in which drift biased control decisions, whether a communications timeout actually occurred during the transfer, or whether all three containers shared both conditions; those gaps are preserved below.

claims.text: Three refrigerated containers exceeded the product temperature limit during a six-hour transfer.
Sensor calibration drifted upward by about 1.5 C, but only while relative humidity exceeded 88%.
The humidity-triggering condition for drift was present during the transfer, for 73 minutes.
A firmware retry defect caused the compressor controller to ignore every second restart command following a communications timeout.
The firmware defect alone was not sufficient to produce a product-limit exceedance, since containers with the defect and calibrated sensors stayed within limit.
The sensor drift alone was not sufficient to produce a product-limit exceedance, since containers with the drift and corrected restart logic stayed within limit.
The exceedance is best explained as a conjunction of sensor drift and the firmware retry defect, with neither factor sufficient alone.
High relative humidity acted as the enabling condition that activated the sensor drift; without it the drift is not stated to occur.
The 45-minute alert suppression window delayed repeat notification after the first acknowledgement.
The delayed alert extended operator response only after the product limit had already been crossed, so it affected excursion duration rather than excursion onset.
The comparison runs function as single-variable controls, which is what licenses the conjunctive reading rather than a single-root-cause reading.
The evidence does not establish the mechanism by which drift plus the retry defect produced the exceedance, only that their co-occurrence tracks it.

relationships.note: Humidity above 88% for 73 minutes supplies the stated trigger condition for drift.
Drift is expressed only through the humidity condition.
Necessary but not sufficient per E7.
Necessary but not sufficient per E6.
E8 places the limit crossing before the delayed operator response.
No evidence that alert suppression influenced whether the limit was crossed; its stated effect is post-crossing.
Co-occurrence is established; the intervening physical mechanism is not.

uncertainties.text: The direction of the control error is unresolved: a sensor reading about 1.5 C high could either mask or exaggerate the true product temperature, and the package does not say whether E1's exceedance was measured or actual.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Paired readings from the drifted sensor and an independent reference probe on the same container during the transfer.

uncertainties.text: It is not stated that a communications timeout actually occurred during the six-hour transfer, so the firmware defect's precondition (E3) may or may not have been triggered.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Controller communication logs for the transfer showing timeout events and subsequent restart commands issued versus executed.

uncertainties.text: Whether all three containers in E1 had both the sensor drift and the firmware defect is not stated.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Per-container configuration and calibration records for the three affected units.

uncertainties.text: The temporal relationship between the 73-minute humidity window (E5) and the limit crossings (E1) is unspecified; overlap is assumed, not shown.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: A time-aligned trace of humidity, product temperature and compressor state across the transfer.

uncertainties.text: The comparison runs (E6, E7) are not described with respect to humidity exposure, route, load or duration, so their status as valid controls for this transfer is uncertain.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Run conditions for the comparison runs, especially whether humidity exceeded 88% and for how long.

uncertainties.text: The magnitude of the exceedance and how far it depended on 1.5 C specifically is unknown, so it is unclear whether a smaller drift would still have combined with the firmware defect to cross the limit.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Recorded peak product temperatures and the numeric product limit for the affected containers.

uncertainties.text: Whether the first acknowledgement that started the 45-minute suppression window (E4) occurred before or after the limit crossing is not stated; E8 places only the extended response after it.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Alert and acknowledgement timestamps alongside the limit-crossing timestamps.

uncertainties.text: No evidence addresses product impact, so whether the exceedance caused loss or harm cannot be determined from this package.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Product stability or disposition data for the affected loads.

actions.text: Correct the firmware retry logic so that no restart command is dropped after a communications timeout; this removes one of the two conjoined factors and E6 indicates the remaining factor alone did not breach the limit.
Recalibrate or humidity-compensate the temperature sensors so drift does not appear above 88% relative humidity; E7 indicates the firmware defect alone did not breach the limit.

Change the alerting rule so that continued or worsening temperature excursions re-alert inside the 45-minute suppression window, which addresses the extended response in E8 without claiming it caused the crossing.
Retrieve per-container records for the three affected units to confirm which had both factors present, resolving U3 before generalising the conjunctive finding.
Pull time-aligned humidity, temperature, communications-timeout and compressor-state traces for the transfer to test the assumed overlap and the untriggered-defect possibility (U2, U4).
Document the humidity conditions of the comparison runs so E6 and E7 can be relied on as controls rather than accepted as stated (U5).

counterfactuals.text: With calibrated sensors and the firmware defect still present, the product limit would not have been exceeded.
With corrected restart logic and the sensor drift still present, the product limit would not have been exceeded.
Had relative humidity stayed at or below 88% throughout, the drift condition stated in E2 would not have been active, and the conjunction required for the exceedance would not have formed.
Had the alerting rule not suppressed repeat alerts, the limit would still have been crossed, but the operator response would have begun sooner and the excursion would likely have been shorter.

Had no communications timeout occurred, the firmware defect's stated trigger would have been absent; the evidence does not settle whether the exceedance would then have been avoided, because it does not confirm a timeout occurred in the first place.
Had the drift been smaller than about 1.5 C with the firmware defect still present, the outcome is undetermined by this package, since no dose-response evidence is supplied.

output.summary: At 09:00 the invoice service began routing legacy-client traffic through a newly enabled adapter configuration, and within two minutes invoice creation errors rose from below 0.2% to 38%. The legacy-client adapter configuration omitted the region-header mapping that the modern-client adapter retained, and 97% of sampled failed requests lacked the region header required by the routing function. Database health indicators stayed within the prior week's normal range, and disabling the new configuration at 09:19 restored the error rate below 0.2% within three minutes. The evidence supports the missing region-header mapping in the legacy-client adapter configuration as the proximate cause; the CPU rise appears to be a correlate rather than a cause, and the 08:54 PDF rendering ticket predates the change and is unconnected by any evidence item.

claims.text: A new legacy-client adapter configuration was enabled for invoice service routing at 09:00.
Invoice creation errors rose from below 0.2% to 38% at 09:02, two minutes after the change.
The dominant failure signature was a missing region header: 97% of sampled failed requests lacked it.
The routing function requires the region header to process a request.
The legacy-client adapter configuration omitted the region-header mapping while the modern-client adapter retained it.
The missing region-header mapping in the new legacy-client adapter configuration caused the invoice creation error spike.
Database error rate, saturation, and replication lag remained within the previous week's normal range, so the database is not implicated.
Disabling the new legacy-client adapter configuration at 09:19 restored errors below 0.2% within three minutes.
Application CPU rose from 51% to 65% during the incident, a moderate increase that remained below saturation.
The CPU rise is more plausibly a downstream correlate of the elevated error/retry traffic than an independent cause; the evidence does not establish its direction.
The 08:54 customer-support ticket about a PDF rendering defect predates the change and no evidence links it to invoice creation failures.
The impact appears scoped to legacy-client traffic, since only the legacy-client adapter configuration lacked the mapping.

uncertainties.text: The remaining 3% of sampled failed requests are unexplained; they may be a second failure mode or background noise.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Error-code and message breakdown for the failures that did carry a region header, compared with the pre-09:00 baseline failure mix.

uncertainties.text: The direction of the CPU relationship is unresolved: the rise from 51% to 65% could be an effect of error handling and retries, or an independent contributor.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: CPU time series aligned minute-by-minute with the error rate across 09:00-09:22, plus profiling or request-volume data showing whether retries drove the load.

uncertainties.text: Why the legacy-client adapter configuration omitted the region-header mapping is unknown (authoring error, intentional removal, or template/default gap).
uncertainties.resolvedBy: The change record and diff for the adapter configuration, with its review and approval history.

uncertainties.text: Whether any invoice creation failures were silent, partial, or produced duplicate or corrupt records is unknown.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Reconciliation of invoice records created between 09:00 and 09:22 against upstream request logs.

uncertainties.text: Whether the 08:54 PDF rendering defect shares any component with the invoice routing path is unknown; the evidence only gives its timestamp and subject.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: The ticket's affected-component and stack-trace details, and whether the PDF path reads the region header.

uncertainties.text: Whether the same missing-mapping pattern exists in other configurations not covered by this evidence is unknown; only legacy-client and modern-client adapters are described.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: An inventory of all adapter configurations checked for the region-header mapping.

uncertainties.text: The detection and decision timeline between 09:02 and the 09:19 disable is not described, so the 17-minute gap cannot be attributed.

actions.text: Add the region-header mapping to the legacy-client adapter configuration to match the modern-client adapter, and re-enable only after verifying the header is present end to end.
Make the routing function fail loudly and explicitly on a missing region header, with an error signature that names the missing field, so the same defect is diagnosable in seconds.
Audit every adapter configuration for required-field mappings, including the region header, rather than treating this as a single-configuration fix.
Gate configuration changes of this kind behind a staged rollout with an automatic error-rate abort, so a 38% error rate cannot persist for 19 minutes.
Reconcile invoices attempted between 09:00 and 09:22 to identify affected legacy clients and confirm no partial or duplicate records were created.
Triage the 08:54 PDF rendering ticket separately; keep it out of this incident's causal account unless component evidence links them.

counterfactuals.text: Had the legacy-client adapter configuration included the region-header mapping, the routing function would have received the header it requires and the error spike would very likely not have occurred.
Had the new configuration not been enabled at 09:00, errors would have stayed near the pre-change baseline, as shown by the return below 0.2% once it was disabled.
Had the change been rolled out to a small fraction of legacy-client traffic first, the blast radius would have been far smaller than 38% of invoice creations.
Had the database been the cause, disabling the adapter configuration would not have resolved the errors within three minutes, and database indicators would not have stayed normal.
Had application CPU been the cause, disabling the adapter configuration would not by itself explain recovery, and a rise to only 65% is weak grounds for a 38% failure rate.
Had the PDF rendering defect been causal, errors would have been expected to rise from 08:54 rather than at 09:02, immediately after the configuration change.

output.summary: The temperature-limit exceedance during the six-hour transfer is best explained by the combined presence of humidity-triggered sensor drift and defective compressor restart handling. Each condition alone was insufficient in the comparison runs. Alert suppression did not cause the initial crossing but extended operator response after it occurred.

claims.text: Three refrigerated containers exceeded the product temperature limit during the transfer.
Relative humidity remained above the sensor-drift threshold for 73 minutes.
During that high-humidity interval, sensor calibration drifted upward by about 1.5 C.
After communications timeouts, the firmware defect caused every second compressor restart command to be ignored.
The evidence supports an interaction between sensor drift and defective restart logic as a contributor to the limit exceedance.
Neither the firmware defect with calibrated sensors nor sensor drift with corrected restart logic produced a limit exceedance in the comparison runs.
The alerting rule suppressed repeated temperature alerts for 45 minutes after acknowledgement.
Alert delay prolonged operator response after the product limit had already been crossed, so it was an aggravating recovery factor rather than the demonstrated cause of the initial crossing.

uncertainties.text: The evidence does not state how upward sensor drift interacted with restart control to produce an actual product-temperature exceedance.
The evidence does not identify the communications-timeout frequency, restart-command sequence, or compressor downtime in the affected containers.
The evidence does not distinguish independently measured product temperature from temperature inferred through the drifting sensors.
The evidence does not establish whether faster operator response could have reduced the duration or severity of the exceedance.
No evidence identifies additional contributors or explains why exactly three containers were affected.

actions.text: Correct the compressor restart logic so restart commands are not discarded after communications timeouts.
Correct or compensate for humidity-dependent sensor calibration drift above 88% relative humidity.
Validate the combined corrections under transfer conditions that include humidity above 88% and communications timeouts.
Revise the repeated-alert suppression behavior to avoid a 45-minute loss of visibility after acknowledgement.
Use an independent temperature reference to determine whether future threshold crossings reflect actual product temperature or humidity-induced sensor bias.

counterfactuals.condition: If sensors had remained calibrated while the firmware defect persisted,
counterfactuals.expectedOutcome: the product limit would not have been exceeded under the comparison-run conditions.

counterfactuals.condition: If restart logic had been corrected while the sensor drift persisted,
counterfactuals.expectedOutcome: the product limit would not have been exceeded under the comparison-run conditions.

counterfactuals.condition: If repeated alerts had not been suppressed,
counterfactuals.expectedOutcome: operator response could have begun sooner after the crossing, but the evidence does not show that the initial crossing would have been prevented.

counterfactuals.condition: If humidity had not exceeded 88%,
counterfactuals.expectedOutcome: the specified humidity-triggered sensor drift would not have occurred; whether the firmware defect alone would then cause an exceedance in this transfer is not directly established.

output.summary: Queue depth grew for 27 minutes without an increase in arrival rate, while consumer throughput fell ~40%, indicating a consumer-side slowdown rather than a load surge. Two candidate causes were introduced in the preceding hour (a consumer-library upgrade and a database index rebuild), and the logs contain signals consistent with each (lock-wait messages and deserialization warnings). The available evidence cannot attribute the stall to either change individually: the only recovery observation reverted both changes together, no single-revert run exists, telemetry does not separate database-wait time from deserialization-retry time, and no traces were retained. The supported conclusion is that one or both of the two changes caused the throughput loss, with the split between them unresolved.

claims.text: The backlog growth was caused by reduced consumer processing capacity, not by increased incoming load.
Consumer throughput dropped roughly 40% over the same 27-minute window in which queue depth rose.
Two changes in the preceding hour are temporally eligible as causes: a consumer-library upgrade and a database index rebuild.
At least one of the two changes caused the throughput loss, since reverting both restored normal throughput.
The evidence does not determine whether the library upgrade, the index rebuild, or both together produced the slowdown.
Increased lock-wait messages are consistent with database-side contention, which the index rebuild could plausibly produce.
Increased deserialization warnings are consistent with a message-decoding regression, which the consumer-library upgrade could plausibly produce.
Both log signals rose together, so neither signal on its own discriminates between the two candidate causes.
The instrumentation in place cannot apportion consumer processing time between database waiting and deserialization retries.
No retained traces exist for the incident window, so after-the-fact per-request attribution is not possible from stored data.
The joint revert is a confounded experiment: its outcome is equally consistent with a single-cause and a two-cause explanation.
The evidence does not establish that the observed log warnings, rather than some unmeasured effect of the changes, are the mechanism of the slowdown.

uncertainties.text: Whether the library upgrade, the index rebuild, or their combination caused the throughput loss.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: A run in which exactly one change is reverted (or reapplied) while the other is held fixed, with throughput measured.

uncertainties.text: How consumer processing time divided between database waiting and deserialization retries.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Instrumentation that times database calls and deserialization paths separately within the consumer.

uncertainties.text: Whether the elevated lock-wait and deserialization messages were causally on the critical path or incidental correlates.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Per-message traces or profiles linking the warning events to the slow processing intervals.

uncertainties.text: Whether the two effects were additive, interacting, or whether one was entirely a side effect of the other.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: A factorial test covering both single-change conditions plus the combined condition.

uncertainties.text: Whether an unlisted third factor coincident with the change window contributed.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: A complete change and environment log for the incident window beyond the two changes named.

uncertainties.text: Whether the index rebuild's effect was transient (only during rebuild) or persistent after completion.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Rebuild start and completion timestamps compared against the throughput curve.

uncertainties.text: Whether deserialization warnings represented failed-and-retried work or logged-but-harmless conditions.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Retry and failure counters for the deserialization path, and the warning text semantics.

uncertainties.text: Whether recovery after the joint revert was caused by the revert or by independent resolution over time.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: A control observation of throughput held under the changed configuration past the revert time.

actions.text: Run a single-variable test: reapply one change alone in a controlled environment and measure throughput, then repeat for the other.
Add separate timers for database call wait and deserialization/retry work in the consumer so the two costs can be apportioned.
Enable and retain trace sampling covering the consumer path so a future incident window has per-request evidence.
Reconstruct an exact change timeline, including index-rebuild start and finish times, and align it to the throughput and queue-depth curves.
Instrument deserialization outcomes as counters (attempts, failures, retries) rather than warning text only.
Adopt a change policy that separates independent changes in time so recovery observations are not confounded.

counterfactuals.text: If only the library upgrade had been reverted and throughput had recovered, the upgrade would be identified as sufficient cause and the index rebuild demoted.
If only the index rebuild had been reverted and throughput had recovered, the rebuild would be identified as sufficient cause.
If either single revert had left throughput depressed but both reverts restored it, a joint or interacting cause would be indicated.
If telemetry had separated database wait from deserialization retry time, the dominant cost centre would be visible without any revert experiment.
If arrival rate had risen instead of staying normal, the backlog could have been explained by load rather than by consumer degradation.
If only one of the two log signals had increased, that signal would have pointed to its corresponding change, though still without proof of mechanism.
